video_title: How Big Can a Tornado Actually Get?

Today, we're comparing the scale of the largest tornadoes ever to carve their way across Earth, including one that caused nearly $1 billion in damages and another that injured more than 150 people in minutes. In 2016, during a significant tornado event that ravaged the United States, High Plains, the central Midwest, and parts of the Ohio Valley over 57 tornadoes touched down, the largest of them being May 9th. Fortunately, despite its massive size, most of the damage wasn't to human structures, but to trees. Two people were injured, but thankfully there were no fatalities. Next, we have the Moshannon Forest tornado, the largest tornado that touched down during a tornado event on May 31st, 1985, in Pennsylvania. The event saw 43 tornadoes touched down. Doesn't matter if you're in your car,  home, or even an airplane, tornadoes don't care. They have one thing on their mind: destruction. Today, we'll look at some of the worst-case tornado scenarios and give you tips  on how to survive them and stay on the ground. To do this, I threw myself on the path  of a tornado in six  different locations. But for legal purposes, and my will to live, we simulated it all with the help of Tuxedo Lab’s game Teardown. Let’s just say... it didn't go so well. Every year in the United States, tornadoes cause about 400 million dollars  in damage and kill about 70 people. But first, be sure to like and subscribe for more incredible action-packed survival videos! Before getting swept up, let’s take a look at the different types of tornadoes. This is where the Fujita Scale comes into play. The scale,  named after Dr. T. Theodore Fujita, a meteorologist and professor at the University of Chicago, was created in 1971  to determine the strength and potential danger of different tornadoes. For nearly 40 years, tornadoes were ranked by windspeed, from F0 to F5. The F stands for Fujita. After years of research, the scale was updated in 2007. The new official name  for tornado potency  is the Enhanced Fujita scale, with tornadoes ranked EF0 to EF5. With the most severe wind speeds -- surpassing 320 km/h (200 mph), you can only imagine how much damage an EF5 tornado is capable of. And, although they’re rare, there have been 67 of them recorded worldwide. 59 in the United States alone. Now, before we explore the damages  in our simulation, let's talk about the warning signs of a tornado. Dark or green-coloured skies,   low-lying clouds, large hail stones,  and loud roaring that sounds like a freight train are all reasons to immediately take cover. You should also listen to your local news stations,  an NOAA weather radio station or even the internet to see if any information is available. Tornadoes are common in the United States because of the mix of terrain and environments  across the country. Specifically, warm,  dry air from the southwest, when mixed with warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico and cold air from the northern Rockies,  is a recipe for disaster. The states in the middle of these conditions are the perfect breeding grounds for tornadoes. The area has been named Tornado Alley because it's the most common spot for severe storms. Over a dozen states,  from Texas to South Dakota  and Ohio to Montana, are categorized as tornado-prone states. Most of the activity happens between April and June, so plan your vacation wisely. They can also occur in winter months, although rare,  and can be deadly. In 2022 alone, tornadoes took the lives of 25 people, injured hundreds and caused billions of dollars in damages. But that's not to say tornadoes only occur in the United States. Canada ranks second in the world in terms of tornadoes, with most of them happening in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Ontario. If you're in a house and see a tornado approaching, you’ll want to get to the basement immediately. They’re often the strongest part of a home, and you're less likely to be hit by flying debris. If that's not an option, seek shelter in a small room  on the home's lowest level —ideally in the middle of the home, where there's more structural support from surrounding walls. This could be a bathroom, closet, or hallway. Stay away from windows, doors, and heavy objects. Doors specifically can easily be ripped off and are often a weaker part of a home's foundation. Heavy objects can also be lifted by strong winds, or at the very least fall over, potentially injuring or trapping you. And of course, windows strong winds, glass flying everywhere — not ideal. You'll also want to protect your head, ideally staying under a sturdy table. Use blankets, a mattress, or a sleeping bag to protect your body. Roger and Royce Slatten were sucked out of their house when a tornado with winds exceeding 265 km/h (165 mph) ripped through. Alternatively, the safest option is any room or area entirely inside the building, away from the windows. The same goes for an apartment building or any highrise. In 2000, Forth Worth, Texas, was struck by an F3 tornado, which resulted in two deaths and $450 million in damages. The 35-story Bank One tower was significantly damaged. The best thing you can do  is pull over, get out,  and run to the nearest sheltered area. Although cars have airbags, which may help protect you during a storm, shattered windows will be your primary concern. Do what you can  to cover yourself and avoid getting cut. Once the tornado passes, try to get to the nearest sheltered area and be on the lookout for other tornadoes that may be coming your way. Although you'll likely never fly through a tornado —at least, I hope not— there are some safety tips if you run into turbulence, a common occurrence  on most flights. First things first,  fasten your seatbelt. If anything happened, you wouldn't want to be lifted  out of your seat. Listen to the crew and cabin members on board, and try to limit your movement around the aircraft. Stay calm; you're flying with professionals and freaking out may only make things worse. In most cases, the turbulence will pass after a few moments, and you'll arrive at your destination  safe and sound. Sadly, this wasn't the case in the 80s for NLM Cityhopper  Flight 431 and the 17 lost souls on board. Aware of the thunderstorms, the two pilots didn't plan to delay their flight. As far as everyone was concerned, they would fly around it. Unfortunately, as they attempted to fly between two clouds, they got caught in what was considered an F1 tornado at the time. Although it was the second lowest ranking, it was still capable of winds up to 177 km/h (110 mph). The strong winds tore off the right wing  and ignited the plane’s  ruptured fuel tanks. The airliner plunged out of the sky and slammed into the ground, killing everyone on board. So, flying into a tornado is possible, but it's extremely unlikely. Thankfully, we have far better systems now to detect these terrible twisters. Now there's one last scenario we find ourselves in. WALKING through a tornado. It gives you very little protection against flying debris and could even kill you if the bridge were to collapse. Find a sturdy building to take shelter in. Even if the tornado appears to be staying in one spot, it could still be making its way toward you. Imagine being thrown thousands of feet by ferocious winds hurling debris! How would you survive? Well, 19-year old Matt Suter couldn't tell you how, but by a sheer miracle, he managed to stay alive after being thrown over 400 m (1300 ft) in the air. In 2006, 19-year-old Suter was swept up in an EF-2 category tornado in Missouri. It not only took his grandmother's mobile home, but him as well. During the chaotic storm,  Suter was hit in the head  by a lamp and fell unconscious. When he woke up, he was in a field nearly a quarter mile away from where his grandmother's home originally was. The unlikely survival story led to Suter being awarded  a world record for the furthest distance survived in a tornado. I'm sure that's one most people are happy to let him have. All in all,  surviving a tornado is not only possible but very likely, so long as you're prepared. Have an emergency kit, a battery-powered radio, a flashlight, and a plan in case you ever need to get through one. Get into a safe space to shelter yourself until the tornado passes, and don't come out until it's safe. Lastly, if it isn't apparent enough after watching my simulations, don't go anywhere near it. Don't try to chase it with your car or get too close. The further you are, the more likely you'll survive and walk away uninjured. Tornadoes can be devastating, but it's nowhere near the level of damage a hurricane can do.
